clue.text: Composer from New Harlem

indicators.note: something new is a fresh version, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: the New York neighbourhood, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A composer who hails from Harlem, New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Harlem' reads like a place name echoing New York, but 'New' is the signal to rearrange. Gustav MAHLER was the Austrian symphonist.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Mahler was an Austrian composer of symphonies and songs, a straightforward example of the category.

clue.text: Several Roman cardinals Saint copies

parts.note: cardinals are counting numbers; as Roman numerals M, I, M, I and C are several of them
S is the standard abbreviation for Saint

explanation.surface: A saint imitates a group of Roman cardinals of the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinals' suggests churchmen in Rome, but it means cardinal numbers written the Roman way: M (1000), I (1), M, I, C (100).
explanation.definitionFit: To mimic someone is to imitate them, so mimics works as a verb synonym for copies in the third person.

clue.text: Bahrain lot worried about toilet in light craft

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters goes round another
worried means fretted or pulled about, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
loo is an informal British word for a toilet

explanation.surface: A crowd of people from Bahrain fret over the lack of a toilet on a small aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters do not stay in one run: the inserted British toilet word lands just before the final letter. 'Light' means lighter than air, not bright.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot air balloon is an aircraft lifted by heated air, literally lighter than the surrounding atmosphere, hence a light craft.

clue.text: Chained wild animal

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters run loose into a new order

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A wild beast kept on a chain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'wild animal' as one phrase, but 'wild' belongs with 'Chained' as its signal. An ECHIDNA is the spiny anteater of Australia and New Guinea.
explanation.definitionFit: The echidna is a spiny egg-laying mammal of Australia and New Guinea, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Starts to alter bus route in a foreign country

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words
a road is a route

explanation.surface: A tourist asks for the bus to change its route while travelling overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes only the first letters of the next two words, not of the whole phrase; 'route' then stands as a full word.
explanation.definitionFit: Being abroad means being overseas, away from one's home nation, so the adverb matches the phrase.

clue.text: Herb's son protected by legal security?

indicators.note: what is protected is sheltered inside its protector, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: bail is money lodged with a court as security for a defendant's release
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A man called Herb has a son who is safeguarded by some legal guarantee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' reads as a man's name with a possessive, but the ’s is 'is' and Herb is the plant being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is an aromatic culinary plant used in Italian cooking, a straightforward example of a herb.

clue.text: Find cover note somehow cocky

indicators.note: somehow means in some unstated way, so the letters are arranged in some other manner

parts.note: all thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone smugly sure they can track down an insurance cover note.
explanation.walkthrough: A cover note is a temporary insurance certificate, which makes the fodder look like a real errand.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocky describes someone brashly sure of themselves, which is the same as being too self-assured.

clue.text: Stores discontinued, having no heart to make a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the letters travel back the way they came
the heart of a word is its middle, and having none means the central letter is removed

parts.note: something discontinued has been stopped

explanation.surface: Closed shops, lacking spirit, try to reopen.
explanation.walkthrough: STOPPED has seven letters, so its heart is the middle P; dropping it leaves STOPED, which is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a warehouse or storehouse where goods are kept, so depots are stores in the noun sense.

clue.text: Dull Head of Theology cut gospel

parts.note: mat (also matt) describes a dull, non-glossy finish

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
to hew is to cut, as with an axe

explanation.surface: A boring head of theology department cut a gospel from the syllabus.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious reading takes 'Dull Head of Theology' as a person, but Dull and Head of Theology are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew is the first of the four books of the New Testament telling the life of Jesus.

clue.text: Drink — it beats "YMCA" dancing

parts.note: to whisk eggs is to beat them, the verb read without its ending

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places, so they end in a new order

parts.note: the four letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A drink is better than dancing to the Village People's disco hit YMCA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It beats' pretends to mean 'is better than'; in the wordplay it is the verb beat, as in eggs, giving WHISK. A whisky mac is Scotch mixed with ginger wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A whisky mac is a British mixed alcoholic cocktail of Scotch and ginger wine, so it is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Clean seats returned around back of stage

indicators.note: to be returned is to be sent back, so the letters run the other way
around means encircling, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: pews are church seats

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Theatre seats that were sent back get tidied around the rear of the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: PEWS turned round is SWEP, and the E from the end of stage goes inside it, before the P.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweep is to clean a floor with a broom, so the verb is a direct synonym for cleaning.

clue.text: Pound pinched by rebuked infant

indicators.note: something pinched is gripped between two edges, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: chid is an old past tense of chide, to rebuke
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A scolded baby has had a pound stolen from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' suggests stealing, but here it means squeezed: CHID, the archaic past of chide, grips the pound sign L.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a very young person, and child is the general word for a young human being.

clue.text: Criminal harm that primarily involves old British chemicals company

indicators.note: to involve is to enfold or wrap up, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: ill as a noun is harm or misfortune, as in 'wish someone ill'

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a British firm broken up in 2008

explanation.surface: Criminal damage that is mainly the doing of a former British chemicals firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Imperial Chemical Industries was once Britain's biggest chemicals maker, known by its initials; 'involves' means the harm-plus-letter pair wraps round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit means forbidden by law or rules, so as an adjective it matches criminal.

clue.text: Gloomy, small, unnaturally pale bird

parts.note: a black mood is a gloomy one
S is the standard abbreviation for small
wan means pale in a sickly, unhealthy way

explanation.surface: A sombre little bird that looks sickly white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unnaturally pale' reads like a description of the bird, but it is the single word WAN, pale from illness; the joke is that the answer is a black bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The black swan is an Australian waterbird with dark plumage and a red bill, so it is one kind of bird.

clue.text: Spendthrift wife alerts Dicky

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters are out of order

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A spendthrift wife warns someone called Dicky.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a man's name, but it is British slang for dodgy or faulty (a dicky heart), which signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel is a wasteful good-for-nothing who squanders money, so a noun synonym for a spendthrift.

clue.text: Behaves badly in court after a drink

indicators.note: after means following on, so one piece is placed behind the others

parts.note: taken as written
CT is the abbreviation for court
to sup is to drink, especially in small mouthfuls

explanation.surface: A defendant misbehaves in the courtroom after having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the drinking before the misbehaviour, but 'after' only means the drink piece comes last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is an idiom for misbehaving or causing trouble, matching 'behaves badly' in the third person.

clue.text: Irritate weed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to annoy or vex someone
second meaning: a stinging wild plant

explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense comes from the sting of the plant: to nettle someone is to get under their skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for annoying someone and the name of a common stinging plant that gardeners pull up.

clue.text: Element extracted from half of Cava?

definitions.text: Element extracted from half of Cava?

parts.words: Element extracted from half of Cava?
parts.note: surface reading: some ingredient taken out of part of a bottle of Spanish sparkling wine
setter's reading: the first half of the word Cava is two letters that form a chemical symbol

explanation.surface: Some component distilled from half a bottle of Spanish fizz.
explanation.walkthrough: Cava is Spanish sparkling wine; its first two letters, CA, are the chemical symbol of the element wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Calcium is a metallic chemical element, atomic number 20, whose periodic-table symbol is Ca.

clue.text: Off and on, fiddly lines in picturesque scene

indicators.note: switching off and on means every other letter is dropped and the rest kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Intermittent, intricate lines appear in a pretty landscape painting.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters come from 'fiddly' alone; 'lines' is a separate piece, two Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a charming, peaceful pastoral scene or episode, so it fits a picturesque scene.

clue.text: Spear second fish

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second
a pike is a freshwater predatory fish

explanation.surface: Harpoon a second fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Spear' as a verb for fishing; it is the definition, and SPIKE works as that verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike something is to pierce it with a sharp point, the same action as spearing it.

clue.text: Smutty pair of ducks kept in pen

indicators.note: what is kept in something is held within it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, drawn as O, so two ducks are OO

explanation.surface: A dirty-minded pair of ducks locked up in an enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smutty' suggests rude jokes, but smut is also soot, so sooty is its literal sense. A duck is cricket's word for a zero score.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut literally means specks of soot or grime, so smutty in its original sense means blackened with soot.

clue.text: Section of Arctic or, better, Scottish mountain

indicators.note: a section is a cut-out part, so the letters are a run lying inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters from the end of the first word to the middle of the last

explanation.surface: A patch of the Arctic, or better still a Scottish peak.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'or' is there to split the phrase naturally; it is ignored when reading the letters across. A Corbett is a Scottish hill between 2,500 and 3,000 feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Corbetts are a named list of Scottish hills between 2,500 and 3,000 feet high, so each one is a Scottish peak.

clue.text: Friends divided by extremely naïve juries

indicators.note: something divided has another piece driven into it, so the outer piece is split around the inner

parts.note: pals are friends

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Friends find themselves split up by juries that are hopelessly gullible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier on 'naïve'; it means the ends of that word, N and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A jury is a group of people chosen to judge a case, and panel is the general word for such a selected group.

clue.text: Fool shortened her dress

indicators.note: a shortened word has been cut down, so its final letter is lopped off

parts.note: clot is British slang for a fool
taken as written before it is cut

explanation.surface: A silly person took up the hem of her frock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortened her dress' suggests taking up a hem; in fact it cuts the last letter from HER. Clot is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone is to put garments on them, so as a verb it is a synonym for clothe.
